Lose means: something that was yours, or within your reach, is no longer there. Whether it's an object, a person, a game, or an opportunity — if it's gone from your possession, control, or grasp, you've lost it.

1. To no longer have something (misplace or have taken)

This is the most everyday use. You had something. Now you don't know where it is, or it has been taken from you.

  • I always lose my keys. (I misplace them.)
  • She lost her wallet on the bus.
  • He lost his job last month. (It was taken from him.)
  • The company lost millions of rupees.

Notice: losing something doesn't always mean you accidentally dropped it. You can lose a job, lose rights, lose your health — all without any physical dropping.

2. To fail to win

When you compete — in a sport, a game, an election, an argument — and you don't win, you lose.

  • India lost the match by 10 runs.
  • She lost the election.
  • He always loses when he plays chess with me.
  • Our team lost badly.

The opposite of "lose" in this sense is "win."

3. To lose a person (death, separation, or drifting apart)

This is a softer, more emotional use. When someone close to you dies, you "lose" them. You can also lose a friend in the sense of no longer being close to them.

  • She lost her father last year. (He passed away.)
  • They lost many soldiers in the war.
  • I've lost touch with most of my school friends. (We drifted apart.)

4. To fail to keep up with something or someone

If someone is moving, speaking, or progressing, and you can no longer follow or track them, you lose them.

  • The police chased the thief but lost him in the crowd.
  • Sorry, you lost me there — can you explain that again? (I stopped understanding you.)
  • I lost the thread of the conversation. (I stopped following the topic.)
  • She was speaking so fast that I lost track of what she was saying.

5. To waste or fail to use

When time, an opportunity, or an advantage slips away without being used, you lose it.

  • Don't lose time — start now.
  • We lost a great opportunity.
  • He lost his chance to study abroad.
  • There's no time to lose. (We must act immediately.)

6. To shed or get rid of (weight, a habit, a quality)

In everyday informal use, you can "lose" something you want to be free of.

  • I want to lose 5 kilograms before my wedding.
  • You need to lose that attitude.
  • She's trying to lose her bad habits.

Here, "losing" something is actually a goal, not a misfortune.

7. To cause someone else to lose something

Here, "lose" takes a slightly different structure. A person's action causes another person to lose something.

  • That one mistake lost him the match. (Because of that mistake, he lost.)
  • Her rude behavior lost her many friends. (Her behavior caused her to lose friends.)
  • The leaked document lost the company a major contract.

The structure here is: [thing/action] + lost + [person] + [what they lost].

8. To lose yourself in something

This is a beautiful and common phrase. It means to become so deeply absorbed in something that you forget everything else around you.

  • She lost herself in the novel and didn't notice it was midnight.
  • He loses himself in music whenever he's sad.
  • I got lost in thought. (I was so deep in my thoughts that I didn't notice what was happening around me.)

9. To be lost on someone

If a joke, a hint, a lesson, or a point "is lost on someone," it means that person simply did not understand it or was not affected by it.

  • The sarcasm was completely lost on him. (He didn't realize it was sarcasm.)
  • Her advice was lost on her children — they never listened.
  • The beauty of the painting was lost on me. (I couldn't appreciate it.)

10. A clock or watch that "loses" time

A clock "loses" time when it runs slower than it should, falling behind the actual time.

  • My old watch loses five minutes every day.

This is one of the most common spelling mistakes in English, so pay attention.

  • Lose (verb) = to not have, to fail to win. Don't lose hope.
  • Loose (adjective) = not tight, not fixed firmly. This screw is loose.

They look similar, but they are completely different words with completely different meanings. "Lose" has one 'o'. "Loose" has two.

These two words overlap but are not the same.

  • You miss a bus = the bus left before you arrived; you were late.
  • You lose something = it is no longer in your possession.

You would say "I missed the bus", not "I lost the bus."

However, if you're not paying attention in class, you might miss a point and consequently lose the understanding. The two can occur together, but each word refers to something specific.

To put it all together: lose is a verb that captures the experience of no longer having, keeping, or succeeding at something. That "something" can be physical (keys, money), abstract (hope, time, opportunity), relational (a friend, a parent), competitive (a game, an election), or even something unwanted that you intentionally shed (weight, a habit). Across all these uses, the feeling is the same — something that was present or possible is now absent or gone.
